questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in liking bias?
choices: Letting feelings toward a source distort judgment of what is being evaluated
Ignoring relationships completely when judging anything
Assuming all positive emotion is irrational

explanation.gentle: Yes. The feeling toward the source is shaping the verdict too much.
explanation.direct: Correct. Affection or dislike is replacing some of the evidence-led judgment.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. The vibe is hacking the score.

questions.prompt: Why is this bias easy to miss?
choices: Because emotional stance arrives before slower evaluation is finished
Because feelings never affect evidence
Because liking always improves accuracy

explanation.direct: Correct. Warmth or irritation can tilt scrutiny before the evidence is fully reviewed.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The weather arrives before the court opens.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits liking bias?
choices: A favored coworker gets extra credit because people like the person, not because the work clearly earned it
A product is rated after a blind comparison of features only
A teacher uses the same standard for liked and disliked students

explanation.gentle: Yes. The source-feeling is carrying the judgment.
explanation.direct: Correct. Affection is softening scrutiny beyond what the evidence supports.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The favorite is getting emotional credit.

questions.prompt: What makes this bias dangerous in evaluation?
choices: It can hide flaws in liked targets and exaggerate flaws in disliked ones
It proves emotion should never exist in judgment
It means all trust is fake

explanation.gentle: Yes. The same evidence can get softer or harsher treatment depending on feeling.
explanation.direct: Correct. Positive feeling and aversion can distort scrutiny in opposite directions.
explanation.competitive: Right. Warmth hands out discounts and irritation adds penalties.

choices: Because affection can make weaknesses seem smaller and easier to excuse
Because liked people never make mistakes
Because positive emotion turns evidence into certainty

explanation.gentle: Right. Warm feeling can soften how the flaws are seen.
explanation.direct: Correct. Affection can shrink scrutiny and inflate trust.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Charm can put a discount sticker on the flaws.

questions.prompt: What is the practical correction in this chapter?
choices: Separate the object being judged from the feeling toward the source
Ignore all emotional reactions permanently
Trust neutral-seeming sources automatically

explanation.gentle: Yes. The fix is to split the object from the source-feeling.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment reviews the object and the emotional stance separately.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Strip the vibe off the case before you score it.

choices: Feeling toward the source with evidence about the object
Familiarity with memory
Trust with planning

explanation.gentle: Right. The emotional reaction is being mistaken for support.
explanation.direct: Correct. Source-feeling is being confused with direct evidence about the thing under review.
explanation.competitive: Yes. The vibe is smuggling itself into the evidence file.

choices: Because aversion can harden scrutiny beyond what the facts alone justify
Because negative feeling is always more accurate
Because disliked people are always lower quality

explanation.gentle: Yes. Cold feeling can make the same evidence look worse.
explanation.direct: Correct. Aversion can intensify criticism even when the facts are mixed.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Irritation can add a penalty fee to the verdict.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest practical correction in this bias?
choices: Make the verdict survive even after mentally removing liking or dislike toward the source
Treat all personal warmth as deception
Assume all neutral judgments are correct

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter asks you to see whether the judgment still stands without the feeling.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment tests whether the conclusion remains once source-feeling is held aside.
explanation.competitive: Right. Pull the emotional subsidy out and see whether the score can still stand up.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's threshold question?
choices: If I removed my feeling toward this person or source, would the judgment still look the same?
How strong is my feeling toward the source right now?
Which verdict feels most comfortable to hold?

explanation.gentle: Yes. That question separates feeling from the object being judged.
explanation.direct: Correct. It tests whether the verdict survives without the source-feeling attached.
explanation.competitive: That is the cut. Does the case still stand after the vibe gets pulled out of it?
